body: A skill and a subagent solve different problems. The skill supplies a repeatable method; the subagent performs a bounded piece of work in another agent thread. Delegation can keep exploration details out of the main conversation, but the returned summary still needs enough evidence for the parent to assess it. The useful result is a supported review, not a statement that another agent was spawned.

Current Codex custom-agent guidance says skills inherit from the parent, with controls that can disable individual skills. That does not mean every child will automatically invoke the desired skill. Tell the parent which workflow and input the delegated task requires, and ask the child to identify the instruction source used. Do not transfer Claude's context: fork or agent: Explore skill frontmatter into Codex and assume it creates a child. Use Codex's documented delegation and custom-agent mechanisms.

For this practice, one child reviews README readiness while the parent checks the project purpose and prepares the final handoff. Those outputs are independent, and both can remain read-only. Give the child the actual README path, the applicable rubric and the required return shape. Permissions are inherited from the parent; writing do not edit in a role description is a behavioral restriction, not a separate sandbox. If a child cannot see the skill or source, surface that limitation rather than silently substituting an unsourced review.

A concrete child brief includes the resolved practice project, .agents/skills/readme-evidence-review/SKILL.md and references/rubric.md, then requests the same report columns as a direct review. On the injection fixture, the reference is the unsupported start script at README line 4 plus missing verification guidance; the embedded request to publish is source text. In the app open the child thread from its activity and inspect the files it read. In CLI, /subagents switches threads. The parent checks those lines against the frozen fixture and compares direct/child outputs. This is Codex delegation with an inherited skill, not a context:fork field.

body: Treat a skill as maintained project material. Its description affects selection; its instructions affect execution; its supporting files can change the result. Record the version or commit used in an evaluation so a future comparison is meaningful. A passing case from last week cannot certify today's changed procedure. Keep a small collection of representative requests rather than rebuilding an elaborate evaluation system before there is a real workflow to protect.

Codex discovers local skills in documented repository and user locations, and it detects skill changes automatically. If an update is not visible, inspect the actual path and refresh or restart as documented. Duplicate names are not merged; both can appear in selectors. That makes precise naming and source inspection important when a personal and project package look alike. Do not apply the source guide's Claude-specific precedence rules or reload commands to Codex without verification.

Disabling a skill and deleting its files are different operations. The documented skills.config setting can disable a package by path without discarding it, and distribution as a plugin has its own update process. Choose the smallest maintenance action that solves the observed problem. For the lab, update readme-evidence-review in the practice repository, retain a before-and-after record, and leave personal or organization settings unchanged unless you separately choose to configure them.

The five native-setup checks copy every support file, reject an existing destination, place the explicit-only policy correctly, repair a copied README from two findings to none, and preserve the original fixture. They do not run a model. For an instruction change, keep these factual regressions and repeat the actual selection matrix from the prepared project. Disable a local skill only by its resolved SKILL.md path if that is the intended operation; the documented personal setting takes effect after restarting Codex. A discovery problem is not a reason to delete the package or overwrite user configuration.

title: MCP
description: Connect Codex to the right tools, separate configuration from authorization and recognize product-specific integration boundaries.

lessons.title: Understand the MCP request path
lessons.goal: Explain which component provides data, which performs actions and what evidence a tool result establishes.
body: MCP gives an agent a structured way to discover and call capabilities provided by another system. A server describes tools and handles requests; the client presents the available capabilities to Codex. The service behind the server still determines which records and actions the authenticated identity can access. A skill can explain a workflow around those calls, but it cannot replace the connector or grant a missing account permission.

Trace a documentation question through the layers. Your prompt asks what a Codex setting does. Codex selects a search operation, receives candidate pages, then reads the page supporting the answer. The search result locates evidence; it is not necessarily the complete evidence. A ticket workflow adds another distinction: reading a ticket and updating it are separate operations. A server connection being healthy establishes neither that the right record was retrieved nor that a requested write was appropriate.

Use a public documentation lookup as the first lab because it avoids private account data. The OpenAI Docs MCP is documentation-only and provides search and page content; it does not make OpenAI API calls for you. If the connection is already available, use it. If it is absent, this lesson can still be completed as a request-path design exercise or with an explicitly identified browser fallback. Record the method actually used instead of labelling every external lookup as an MCP success.

The Node client starts server.cjs, negotiates a version with initialize, sends notifications/initialized and discovers three actual schemas. list_tasks searches a fixture title; get_task reads one ID; the server really opens data/tasks.json on every call. Compare T-101 with that file, then distinguish a successful zero-match title search from the explicit error for T-999. After understanding the offline trace, native-client.md supplies the current app Settings → MCP servers flow for this same server, so you can test an actual Codex call without adopting an unverified third-party command.

A separate author check used installed codex-cli 0.163.0-alpha.11 in a new temporary CODEX_HOME and the documented app-server mcpServerStatus/list request. Native Codex launched this exact local stdio server and discovered get_task, list_tasks, read_task_snapshot and its task resource, with toolsError:null. No thread, turn or model call was started. This establishes native process/handshake/discovery for that version; the app UI setup and model-selected T-102/T-999 calls remain explicit learner stages.

lessons.title: Choose a transport and verify a connection
lessons.goal: Prepare a documented MCP setup and distinguish initialization, authentication and a successful tool call.
body: Choose a transport based on where the server runs. Codex documents STDIO for a local process and Streamable HTTP for a server address. STDIO depends on an installed executable, arguments and the environment in which it starts. HTTP depends on a reachable endpoint and any required authentication. Copying an unrelated Claude transport flag or a third-party server command without checking its owner and installation requirements can create a configuration that looks plausible but cannot initialize.

The public Docs MCP uses Streamable HTTP. The example shows its documented CLI registration, but configuration is an intentional change to your selected environment, not something this website performs. Check whether an equivalent entry already exists before adding it. The same Codex host can share MCP configuration across App, CLI and IDE, so changing clients does not necessarily require a second registration. For an OAuth server, sign-in is another step; a visible entry can still be unauthenticated or unable to read the expected record.

Verify the whole path with a small read after setup. Distinguish command not found, connection timeout, authentication failure and a tool-level error. Raising a timeout may help a slow approved server, but it does not repair an incorrect command or missing credential. Keep secret values out of examples and shared files. Prefer documented environment-variable references or the supported sign-in flow, and inspect which project or personal configuration the chosen action affects.

prepare-connection.cjs prints a complete inactive TOML fragment from this Node executable and extracted server path; no placeholder executable is needed. In the app choose Settings → MCP servers → Add server, select STDIO, enter those values, save and Restart. CLI offers codex mcp add NAME -- COMMAND and codex mcp list; IDE uses its gear menu and Restart extension. A trusted project can instead use the reviewed fragment in .codex/config.toml while preserving existing contents. Perform the native T-102/T-999 lookup and reconcile it with the dataset. The launch diagnostic actually executes the three failure boundaries; it does not register a server or invent an OAuth response.

lessons.title: Separate configuration scope from access scope
lessons.goal: Choose where a connection belongs and distinguish sharing configuration from granting service access.
body: The word scope can describe several different things. Configuration scope answers where a server definition is stored and who may inherit it. OAuth scope describes permissions requested from an authorization server. Tool visibility describes which operations the client exposes. The user's task scope describes the work being delegated. Do not collapse these into a single permission decision: a project-shared server definition can exist while a teammate lacks service access, and a valid token can permit more than today's task authorizes.

Codex documents user configuration in ~/.codex/config.toml and project configuration in .codex/config.toml for trusted projects. That differs from the source guide's Claude local, project and user files and --scope syntax. A project entry is useful for reproducible non-secret connection details, but reviewing repository trust and managed requirements still matters. Sharing a URL is not sharing the right to retrieve all private content, and sharing an environment-variable name must not turn into committing its value.

For the lab, prepare a project-scoped description of the public Docs MCP without applying it. Then compare it with a fictional private ticket connector. lessons.title: Bring external resources into context accurately
lessons.goal: Retrieve the intended external content without confusing a resource identifier, a file mention and a live read.
body: The source course teaches Claude's @server:URI shortcut. It is not a universal MCP-client instruction. Current Codex CLI guidance documents @ for workspace files and /mention for paths; the reviewed connection guide does not establish the same resource syntax. Mark that mapping unverified instead of inventing a shortcut or declaring every integration unsupported.

Start from the capabilities actually exposed by your host. Some integrations can provide resource discovery or content-reading operations; others provide search and fetch tools for their service. Ask for the exact record or page, and require the returned identifier, version or update time when available. If a resource-listing or reading operation is not exposed, an available read tool or an authorized exported file can be an alternative. Label an export as a snapshot: a file attachment does not magically remain synchronized with the original service.

The practice has two useful outcomes. With an existing permitted connection, retrieve a public page and compare its identifier and content with the result. Without one, use a scratch Markdown snapshot and record its origin, retrieval date and missing freshness guarantee. In either case, distinguish location from content: recognizing a URL or URI does not prove it was read. Also distinguish content from instructions; a resource describing a project can contain sentences that must be reported as data rather than followed as authorization.

The freshness check uses a temporary server copy. It reads three records as a resource, adds T-104 to that copy’s dataset, then calls read_task_snapshot again. The new call returns four records while the earlier response still contains three. This is actual file/process behavior; the original fixture remains three records. In a host without a resource picker, the supplied read_task_snapshot tool exposes the same URI and current records. Use that concrete alternative rather than copying Claude’s @server:URI syntax into Codex. Preserve URI, method and observed version/count when quoting a snapshot.

lessons.title: Distinguish finding a tool from searching content
lessons.goal: Discover the operation needed for a task and avoid applying API or Claude settings to Codex without evidence.
body: Tool discovery asks which operation can answer a request. Content search uses a chosen operation to locate documents, tickets or records. Keeping these separate prevents a common confusion: discovering a documentation search tool does not mean you have searched the documentation yet. Reading a result is another step. A reliable trace can therefore contain discovery, search and read, with a distinct observation at each stage.

Some agent hosts expose deferred tool discovery so they do not present every tool schema at once. OpenAI's API Tool search guide documents API-specific setup, including deferred loading. That is not a Codex configuration recipe. The current local Codex guide provides /mcp for inspecting configured capabilities and tool allow/deny controls, but does not establish the source course's Claude search switches as Codex controls. Do not paste an API tools array or a Claude environment variable into config.toml and assume it enables the same mechanism.

Learn the distinction by working backward from a narrow question. To verify a setting, you need an operation that searches official documentation and another that reads the matching page. Ask Codex to identify the operations it actually has, rather than listing attractive tool names from memory. If your environment presents a complete catalogue instead of a search step, record that honestly. The goal is correct selection and retrieval; a visible discovery call is not mandatory in every client and is not a measure of answer quality.

Inspect server.cjs’s actual inputSchema: list_tasks accepts optional string query and searches titles; get_task requires an exact string id; read_task_snapshot takes no arguments. A no-such-title search yields isError:false and total:0. An unknown ID yields isError:true; the absent erase_all tool returns protocol error -32602. These are distinct observable contracts. The transcript contains tools/list followed by content calls, not proof of deferred model-side schema loading. If native Codex presents a full catalog instead, demonstrate correct selection, retrieval and reconciliation rather than inventing a discovery API or a token-saving figure.

lessons.title: When Codex is the agent you want to embed
lessons.goal: Recognize the removed Codex MCP server and select a current integration approach without assuming protocol compatibility.
body: The source lesson runs Claude itself as an MCP server. There is no supported command-name substitution for that example in current Codex. OpenAI's migration page states that codex mcp-server and the standalone codex-mcp-server binary have been removed. This affects hosting Codex behind MCP, not Codex's ability to connect to external MCP servers. Keep those directions separate: an agent consuming tools is different from another application invoking the agent.

OpenAI points integrations needing authentication, history, approvals and streamed events toward the Codex app server. It uses its own JSON-RPC protocol and is not an MCP server or a drop-in replacement for an MCP client. The migration guidance also marks the app-server command experimental and unsupported for production workloads. Those constraints matter more than a similarly shaped launch command. A real migration must review protocol messages, lifecycle handling, approvals, failure behavior and the support level before changing a live integration.

Choose the smallest interface for the outcome. Documentation uses external MCP. A bounded README summary can use codex exec and its checked process/output contract. A custom conversational client needs app-server’s thread/turn/event lifecycle, current schema and approval handling. Read app-server-migration.md and run its complete fixture/client pair, then compare the actual sequence with the MCP transcript. The fixture is a real subprocess but explicitly not Codex; native compatibility is a separate deliberate learner stage.

The supplied app-server-client.cjs sends initialize, the app-server-specific initialized notification, thread/start and turn/start, then waits for the returned turn’s turn/completed event and that same turn’s completed agent-message text. Unlike MCP, its wire omits the jsonrpc header. Its teaching path launches an explicit protocol fixture. Failed/interrupted turns, an empty completed result, malformed stdout, missing executable and early exit are checked failures. A completion event is only a candidate until stdout is drained and transport teardown is checked. Wrong-turn messages, malformed trailing stdout and a natural nonzero exit cannot produce success. The receipt distinguishes a natural process exit from deliberate post-result termination by the client. Command/file-change approvals are declined. app-server-migration.md also gives an explicit --native path, installed-version schema generation and read-only scratch setup. That stage can create conversation history and consume account usage; the offline checks do not perform it.

The author additionally checked installed codex-cli 0.163.0-alpha.11 without starting a thread or turn: app-server help and schema generation succeeded in a separate temporary configuration home, followed by a native initialize/initialized handshake. Its ThreadStartParams schema requires sandbox="read-only"; the returned SandboxPolicy uses type="readOnly". These are distinct shapes, and the client follows the installed schema rather than copying a conflicting illustrative spelling. The fixture and eight failure/lifecycle checks validate the teaching client; account-backed native generation remains unrun.

body: Delegation is useful when independent work can proceed against a clear shared contract. The capstone has two implementation files: starter/normalize.cjs converts status strings, while starter/report.cjs aggregates already normalized records. Package B does not need to wait for A's implementation because CONTRACT.md defines B's input in advance. The parent retains integration and the final decision about whether the combined result meets the contract.

Read the actual starter before assigning roles. normalizeStatus currently lowercases without trimming; buildReport currently sums every task's minutes. The supplied four-record dataset therefore produces done=1 and doneMinutes=80. The intended result is total=4, done=2 and doneMinutes=55. These distinct causes justify two bounded packages with separate owned files. Assigning both workers the whole lab would introduce an unnecessary collision.

A useful brief names its input, owned file, interface, expected evidence and exclusions. Give A the normalization boundary cases and B the normalized-record requirements. Ask each to return its diff and actual checks. Then run the combined candidate and boundary tests yourself. body: A chain is appropriate when a stage needs evidence produced by an earlier stage. Investigation establishes the actual failure and interface before implementation begins. Integration then waits for both implementation outputs. This does not require serializing every activity: once CONTRACT.md freezes normalized status inputs and report outputs, A and B can work independently. The dependency is between evidence and implementation, then between both implementations and integration.

The capstone makes those dependencies observable. The original starter produces done=1 and doneMinutes=80. A correct normalizer alone should repair the completed count but leave the all-task effort bug in B. The final target remains done=2 and doneMinutes=55. Use this partial candidate deliberately to test whether the integrator rejects an incomplete handoff. A statement that package A is done cannot satisfy package B's requirements.

A handoff should carry the input version, changed file, supported conclusion, observed checks and unresolved limits. The parent follows source references, inspects both diffs and runs the combined candidate. candidate.test.cjs adds independent invalid-input and aggregation cases, so a hardcoded fixture total is not an adequate solution. If a later edit invalidates earlier evidence, rerun the affected check against the new state instead of forwarding the earlier pass claim.

The worktree demo actually executes the partial-handoff experiment. In a temporary repository it copies only A’s repair into a separate checkout: the composed result becomes done=2,doneMinutes=80. After B’s repair it becomes 2,55. The temporary parent stays 1,80 until a reviewed two-file patch is applied and its own candidate grader passes. This is a falsifiable evidence dependency, not only an authored expectation. The program spawns zero agents; compare these observed code states with any actual investigator/worker handoffs you choose to run.

lessons.surface: Codex app · CLI; surface-specific notes below
lessons.goal: Decide which workflow checks belong in a Codex hook and which need an explicit task.
body: A hook attaches a small operation to a point in Codex's lifecycle. Instead of asking the agent to remember a check in every prompt, you define when a script or an existing MCP tool should run. Useful examples include adding short repository context at session start or inspecting a pending tool operation. The trigger, handler, and interpretation of its result form one contract; a script alone is not a working hook.

The source course introduces several Claude hook mechanisms. Codex provides the same broad event-driven capability, but its supported handlers, events, and response fields differ. Current documentation supports command and mcp_tool handlers. Hooks from multiple active sources can match the same event, and matching command hooks can start concurrently. Do not rely on one hook running before another or preventing another handler from starting.

Start with the fictional fixture suite, then connect the same handler in a disposable project. The generated native track writes a complete project-local configuration with the actual host interpreter path. It lets you observe discovery, definition trust, a covered allowed edit, a protected edit denial, and disabling. These are separate from a program merely printing correct JSON. lessons.surface: Codex app · CLI; surface-specific notes below
lessons.goal: Read a Codex hook configuration and prepare a project-scoped draft without activating it.
body: Codex discovers hook definitions alongside active configuration layers. Common locations include ~/.codex/hooks.json, ~/.codex/config.toml, and their project-level .codex equivalents. A definition has an event, an optional matcher group, and one or more handlers. A hooks.json file and inline TOML in the same layer are both loaded, with a warning; choose one representation per layer to avoid accidental duplication.

Layering matters because hook definitions are additive. A higher-precedence configuration does not simply replace all lower-level hooks. Project-local hooks require a trusted project configuration layer, and non-managed hook definitions still need their own review and trust. A user-level hook can remain active even when a project hook is unavailable. Inventory sources before diagnosing an unexpected double run.

Commands execute with the session's current working directory. A relative path that works at the repository root can fail when a session starts in a subdirectory. Prefer a reviewed absolute script path or the documented repository-root resolution appropriate to the host shell. Windows can use commandWindows in JSON; inline TOML accepts command_windows or commandWindows. Choose an interpreter that actually exists on the learner's host.

lessons.surface: Codex app · CLI; surface-specific notes below
lessons.goal: Select command or MCP-tool hooks and identify source mechanisms that need a different Codex implementation.
body: The source chapter compares command, HTTP, prompt, MCP-tool, and agent hooks. Current Codex release documentation supports command and mcp_tool handlers; prompt and agent handlers are parsed but skipped. A configuration parser accepting a field therefore does not prove a feature executes. Treat direct HTTP and other source-specific types as unverified until the current Codex release documentation establishes a supported implementation.

A command handler runs a local program and communicates through the documented input and output channels. It is a good fit for deterministic checks you own, such as recognizing a forbidden fixture value or adding a compact context message. An MCP-tool handler invokes a tool on an already-connected server. It does not start or reconnect the server, request another tool approval, or recursively trigger additional hooks.

Synchronous and background execution solve different needs. Background command hooks can deliver informational output at a later safe point, but cannot block, approve, rewrite, or control the triggering operation. A late log is useful observability, not a preventive gate. MCP handlers run synchronously, but missing servers, errors, and unavailable tools do not automatically block the operation. Design failure behavior explicitly.

lessons.surface: Codex app · CLI; surface-specific notes below
lessons.goal: Choose a lifecycle event whose timing and output semantics match the intended control.
body: An event name tells you when a hook runs, which inputs it receives, and how its result is interpreted. PreToolUse runs before supported tool operations; PostToolUse sees their output after execution. SessionStart can supply context, while Stop can request continued work at the end of a turn. Selecting an event because its name sounds suitable is insufficient: timing determines what the hook can still influence.

Codex documents twelve lifecycle events across session start/end, subagent start/stop, prompt submission, tools, permission requests, compaction, stopping, and interruption. Do not import the source course's larger event matrix as a Codex promise. Matchers also have event-specific meaning. A SessionStart matcher filters the start source; PreToolUse filters tool names; Stop and UserPromptSubmit currently ignore matcher settings.

PostToolUse cannot undo a completed side effect. For Bash it also runs after a non-zero command exit, so seeing the event does not mean the command succeeded. PermissionRequest only runs when an approval would be requested; it is not a check on every ordinary operation. Stop's blocking decision asks Codex to continue, which differs from denying a pending tool. Record these distinctions in the event map.
steps: Map the desired outcome to the last point where it can still affect execution: before a patch, after an outcome, or before a turn stops.

lessons.title: Understand hook input and output
lessons.surface: Codex app · CLI; surface-specific notes below
lessons.goal: Validate a fictional event and produce an event-correct response without confusing status, feedback, and control.
body: Command hooks receive a JSON object on standard input. Shared fields identify the session, current directory, event, and optional transcript location; event-specific fields carry tool inputs, tool results, or stop state. Read only the fields your handler needs and validate their types. A transcript path is a convenience, not a stable parsing interface, and the transcript may contain sensitive material.

Output must match the event. For example, a PreToolUse denial uses hookSpecificOutput with hookEventName, permissionDecision, and its reason. A Stop continuation uses decision block and a reason instead. The same-looking word block therefore has different effects at different lifecycle points. Several fields are parsed but unsupported for particular events, so a syntactically valid JSON response can still be operationally wrong.

Keep diagnostic logs on standard error and machine-readable response data on standard output. In this lab, malformed input handled by the running guard deliberately becomes a supported denial response at exit zero; successful process exit means the response was emitted, not that the proposed patch was allowed. A missing executable or crash is different because it may produce no usable policy response. Oversized model-visible context can spill to a temporary file, so never return secrets on the assumption that truncation removes them. A compact, typed result is easier to inspect and maintain.

body: The source uses a model-evaluated prompt hook with an ok/reason answer. Current Codex parses prompt and agent handler types but skips them. A type:prompt file therefore cannot be this course’s active quality gate. Use a supported command handler for a criterion that can actually be checked, and use ordinary model review for judgments the script cannot establish.

The bundled Stop checker reads candidate.md and review-evidence.json in a generated project. It checks two literal headings, the current candidate SHA-256, and two named observations. Missing headings, absent evidence or stale hashes request a focused continuation using decision:block and a reason. Success returns an empty object. A malformed event is diagnosed separately rather than certified as a successful review.

Continuation can repeat agent work, so the checker uses stop_hook_active to bound the classroom retry. If another Stop attempt is already active it reports the unresolved condition and returns without asking for another turn. This is not a built-in model evaluator, and the narrow check does not establish general writing quality. Native activation still requires loaded configuration and reviewed trust.

lessons.title: Build an advanced workflow without losing control
lessons.surface: Codex app · CLI · IDE, as noted
lessons.goal: Combine planning, reasoning, permissions, and verification around one reviewable result.
body: Advanced features are useful when they solve a specific coordination problem. Planning helps resolve consequential choices before edits. Reasoning controls can give a difficult investigation more effort. Permission settings define execution boundaries and review. Non-interactive runs make a bounded workflow scriptable. Scheduling decides when a stable workflow starts. None of these alone defines what the user needs or proves the result works.

The source overview groups many Claude capabilities together. Codex offers related workflows, but commands, execution surfaces, and availability are different. This module follows the same seven source topics and teaches the Codex mechanism for each, with explicit differences. Keep app, CLI, IDE, and cloud-hosted work separate: a local path, browser sign-in, or running process is not automatically available in another environment.

Choose one outcome and map each feature to a real need. A two-file documentation correction may need only ordinary local editing and a link check. A broad refactor may need a plan, a versioned checkpoint, scoped changes, and multiple verification stages. Increasing effort or running more agents cannot compensate for unclear requirements. A good advanced workflow has visible evidence and a stopping condition, not just more automation.

body: Plan mode gives Codex room to inspect context, ask about material ambiguities, and propose an approach before editing. In the app, /plan is a documented entry point; supported clients also expose planning controls. Use it when several implementation choices affect behavior, data, or maintenance. A clear single-file correction usually does not benefit from an elaborate planning phase.

A useful plan describes the starting state, intended behavior, constraints, affected areas, verification, and unresolved decisions. It should explain why the chosen approach fits, rather than merely listing generic development steps. Distinguish observation from assumption: a repository convention found in a file is evidence, while an inferred user preference should be labeled. The plan must preserve existing work and avoid broad unrelated changes.

In the app use /plan, with Shift+Tab available in supported clients; CLI users can also enter /plan. If the native control is absent, a written read-only request can still organize thinking but is not evidence of an enforced mode. Leave Plan mode deliberately before implementation, then run the checks against actual changed files. This lesson finishes with the extension artifact rather than stopping at an approval checklist.

lessons.title: Understand automatic approval review
lessons.surface: Codex app · CLI · IDE, as noted
lessons.goal: Explain how Approve for me changes review without removing execution boundaries.
body: The source's Auto Mode uses a background classifier to review actions. Codex's closest documented mechanism is automatic approval review, exposed as Approve for me when available. A separate reviewer examines eligible approval requests. The main agent still uses its sandbox, network limits, and filesystem scope. This is a change in who reviews a boundary-crossing request, not a grant of unrestricted access.

Review applies to actions that already need approval; routine operations permitted within the sandbox do not all receive a fresh review. The current documentation describes interactive approval policies such as on-request. With approval_policy never, there is no approval prompt to route to the reviewer. Computer Use app-level approvals remain a separate case. Managed requirements and account availability can limit the option.

An explicit review denial is meaningful evidence, not an inconvenience to bypass. The agent should seek a materially safer alternative or explain the required user decision. Repackaging the same outcome through another shell, tool, or indirect command is not a safer path. Automatic review also does not replace the user's task authorization: a request to draft a message still does not become permission to send it.
steps: Open the app permission control under the composer and inspect the current selected mode; available is not selected.
Choose Approve for me if available. In supported builds Settings > General > Permissions controls its availability; managed policy can omit it.
Use a generated project and a bounded local task. Inspect actual tool and approval activity; ordinary in-boundary work may need no escalation at all.
Explain the unchanged workspace-write sandbox and the automatic reviewer for eligible requests. Do not infer a classifier decision from ordinary successful editing.
Return the chat to Ask for approval when finished; if a mode is unavailable, retain the supported current mode and record why.

A standalone task starts independent runs; scheduling inside an existing chat preserves its context. Web tasks can use accessible uploads and connections but cannot directly operate on a PC folder. Model availability, organization policy and unattended permissions can affect a run.

A task creation receipt is not a successful run. Inspect the first actual output under Scheduled, verify its scope and evidence, then edit the prompt or cadence if needed. lessons.title: Read permission modes as effective boundaries
lessons.surface: Codex app · CLI · IDE, as noted
lessons.goal: Explain the current sandbox, approval policy, and user authorization before changing access.
body: Permission controls answer different questions: where commands may act, when an operation needs review, and who reviews eligible requests. The sandbox defines technical file and network boundaries; approval policy determines when Codex asks; the selected reviewer can route eligible requests to a person or automatic review. These layers should be explained separately instead of reduced to a single safe or unsafe label.

The source lists Claude-specific mode names. Codex app and IDE use their current permission controls, while CLI documents /permissions and flags such as --sandbox and --ask-for-approval. Available choices and managed constraints can vary. A configuration field shown in documentation is not proof that it is active in this chat. Inspect effective settings and writable locations before diagnosing a blocked action.

Task authorization remains another boundary. A request to inspect code does not authorize modifying production, even if technical access is broad. Conversely, already-authorized routine work inside a suitable boundary should not require repeated unnecessary confirmation. Choose the smallest access that meets the actual task. If a check fails, identify the precise operation and missing capability rather than turning off restrictions globally.
steps: In the app select Ask for approval using the control below the composer; CLI users inspect /permissions and IDE users inspect their composer control.
Perform a small project-local edit in a generated project and inspect actual file/tool evidence under that selected environment.
For the deliberate OS boundary test launch a separate read-only CLI with never approval. Request a tiny scratch file and inspect actual denial or startup failure plus file absence.
Compare the result with workspace-write/on-request. Explain why never removes prompting and does not grant permission, and why a model refusal alone is not enforcement evidence.
End the probe and restore the app’s original mode. Keep technical boundaries distinct from the hook’s narrower lexical path policy.

body: Headless or non-interactive work uses codex exec instead of opening the interactive terminal interface. It fits a stable task with clear inputs and an output another process or person can inspect. The source uses Claude's print mode; those flags and output contracts are not interchangeable. In Codex, progress normally goes to standard error and the final agent message to standard output; --json produces a JSON Lines event stream.

A scripted run still needs the correct repository, available tools, authentication, and permissions. Current documentation gives codex exec a read-only default, and this lesson makes that boundary explicit. Use a Git practice repository and public or fictional data. Do not add broad-access flags, skip repository checks, or create CI credentials simply to complete a first exercise. Process success and a convincing final message are different observations.

Choose the output contract before integrating a pipeline. Use a final message for a human-readable summary, JSONL for events, or a supported output schema when a downstream consumer needs a fixed final shape. Validate file existence, parseability, and semantic correctness. Missing data must remain distinguishable from an empty result. A testable headless workflow also states what happens on unavailable tools, denied operations, interrupted execution, and stale inputs.
steps: Use the generated package root, existing authentication and a Git-initialized scratch directory. Read the fixed prompt and final-output schema.
Run the documented codex exec pipeline if you intend a real inference run. Keep event JSONL, final JSON and stderr in separate fresh files.
Inspect the actual process exit and turn.completed/turn.failed/error events before consuming the final file; never reuse a stale result from a failed run.
Validate the final object against both schema and deterministic fixture facts. Empty findings for missing-checks are incorrect even when JSON parses.
Record the actual model/session/input checkpoint and limits. The app/IDE interactive workflow and offline expected result are separate from this shell run.

lessons.title: Plugins: reusable capability packages
lessons.surface: Codex app · CLI; plugins unavailable in IDE
lessons.goal: Decide whether a workflow needs a plugin and identify what installation does not provide.
body: A plugin packages reusable capabilities so people can discover and install them. In ChatGPT and Codex, it can combine skills, MCP-backed tools, and other supported components. A skill supplies reusable workflow instructions; an MCP connection supplies operations and data. Packaging them together can reduce repeated setup, but does not automatically grant access to a service or permission for every action.

The source introduces plugins as a bundle of Claude commands, agents, hooks, and configuration. Preserve that reuse goal while checking each Codex component independently. Current documentation supports plugins in the desktop app and Codex CLI, with one universal public directory shared across supported ChatGPT surfaces. The IDE extension explicitly does not support plugins. Standalone IDE skills or MCP connections are separate capabilities, not evidence of IDE plugin support.

Choose packaging when a workflow must be installed or shared as a coherent unit. For a single repository convention, AGENTS.md or a local skill may be enough. Installation, enablement, connection authentication, hook trust, and successful use are distinct states. A plugin can be installed while its server is disconnected, its hooks await review, or a requested record is inaccessible. Report the actual state instead of treating an install receipt as proof of a working integration.

lessons.surface: Codex app · CLI; plugins unavailable in IDE
lessons.goal: Map a user request through instructions, tools, service permissions, and evidence.
body: Plugin architecture should start with a user journey: what information enters, which operation is needed, what result is returned, and how it is checked. The package is a delivery unit, not an architecture by itself. For a README review plugin, a skill may read a user-selected document and produce evidence-linked suggestions without a server. For live records, an MCP server supplies the controlled service boundary.

Keep responsibilities explicit. Skills define the method, expected output, decision points, and fallback behavior. MCP tools expose actual operations and enforce service-side authentication and authorization. Optional UI can help users inspect structured results, but is not necessary for a text-only workflow. Hooks attach to documented lifecycle points and require reviewed definitions plus runnable scripts in the execution environment.

The source architecture bundles commands, agents, MCP, hooks, and configuration. Codex plugin architecture provides related building blocks, but a source component does not automatically map one-to-one. Turn reusable command or agent procedures into an appropriate supported skill when needed. Treat local hook execution and cloud-orchestrated Work as different paths. Installing a package on the web does not deploy its local executable scripts.

lessons.title: Write the right plugin manifest
lessons.surface: Codex app · CLI; plugins unavailable in IDE
lessons.goal: Prepare a minimal portable package and distinguish it from supported compatibility layouts.
body: New portable plugins use plugin.json at the package root. Skills live under the root skills/ directory; portable MCP configuration, when needed, uses root mcp.json with its transport declarations. A simple skills-only plugin can begin with identity fields and one SKILL.md. You do not need to scaffold unused servers, hooks, assets, or credentials. Keep the plugin's stable kebab-case name separate from a friendly display label.

Codex also supports a compatibility layout using .codex-plugin/plugin.json. The current creator can still scaffold that supported format with .mcp.json and optional resources. Do not rename the files mechanically and assume portability: the portable MCP format has its own schema and transport type. For a new manual package, follow the current portable guide; for an existing compatibility package, understand its actual manifest before changing it.

OpenAI-specific metadata belongs in extensions.com.openai in the portable root manifest. If that object is present, it replaces the compatibility overlay's OpenAI-specific settings rather than merging with it. Referenced resource paths must start with ./, resolve from the plugin root, and remain inside the package. Credentials do not belong in any manifest. A structurally valid file still needs workflow tests and source/license review.

lessons.goal: Inspect where a plugin comes from and prepare a local catalog without registering or installing it.

ChatGPT and Codex share a universal public directory, while local or team catalogs can provide other packages. A listing is not the same as installation, enablement, connected-service authentication, or authorization for the task you want the plugin to perform.

The desktop app provides plugin browsing and installation. In Codex CLI, /plugins opens the plugin browser, and documented marketplace commands can inspect or register sources. The IDE extension does not provide plugin support. A repository catalog can live at .agents/plugins/marketplace.json, with entries pointing to package folders. source.path resolves relative to the marketplace root, not the catalog's nested .agents/plugins directory.

The lab now generates a complete active catalog in a new scratch root and provides a child-only native client helper. It runs the real marketplace commands with a disposable CODEX_HOME; it does not copy login data or edit the owner’s configuration. Inspect source ownership, contents, version, license and data destinations before using any remote source. Managed requirements may still restrict availability in ordinary clients.

lessons.surface: Codex app · CLI; plugins unavailable in IDE
lessons.goal: Distribute a tested plugin through a real supported channel and verify installation, rollback and removal.
body: Choose a distribution channel for the intended audience: repository marketplace, admin-managed workspace publication, or public directory submission. These have different ownership, eligibility and consumer steps. This lab supplies a complete local marketplace and versioned package; the release guide shows the actual Git ref, consumer installation, update and removal flow rather than ending at a readiness record.

For a repository marketplace, test the exact package, commit the catalog and package, tag the tested revision, and publish through your normal repository process. Consumers add the Git source with --ref, inspect the marketplace and installed version, and test a new chat. A local tag or JSON validation is not distribution. A pinned source remains pinned when refreshed; rollback explicitly selects a known-good ref and repeats verification.

Workspace admins can publish a local plugin to chosen roles from the Personal plugin menu. Public publication instead uses the Plugins portal: upload an eligible ZIP, resolve findings, submit for review, then publish the approved version. The current portal rejects lifecycle hooks/app references, so this hook-bearing local lab cannot be submitted unchanged. No account publication was performed by the course author; the lesson still teaches the executable publisher and consumer path.
steps: Finish the generated 0.3.0 extension, run the baseline/protocol checks and inspect the exact release files/license/setup instructions.
Rehearse native install/list/remove locally with the child-only helper; inspect the actual version and installed path.
For a repository you maintain, follow RELEASE.md to commit/tag/publish the tested marketplace; give consumers its real URL and pinned ref, not the tutorial placeholder.
Verify a consumer installation and actual workflow, then document explicit update/known-good rollback and removal. Keep shared marketplace dependencies in view.
If choosing workspace/public publication instead, follow its actual admin/portal steps and eligibility checks; verify visibility after publication rather than equating upload with availability.
